---
title: "Network from Lines: How Connected Is Connected"
date: 2026-09-13
categories: [article, network, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre: turn a line layer into a graph, and see how a few meters of tolerance change how many pieces the network actually has."
---

A road network, a river system, a set of pipelines: any layer of
lines is only a *network* once you decide which endpoints count as
the same junction. Two segments that were meant to meet but miss by a
few centimeters (a common noding gap in real data) become two
separate, disconnected pieces of the graph unless you tell the
algorithm how close is "close enough." That single decision, a snap
tolerance in meters, can change how many disconnected pieces a
network has without changing a single coordinate.

Want to explore this interactively, with an adjustable tolerance and
the graph drawn directly on the map? Use the [standalone
tool](/tools/network-from-lines.html): same idea, adjustable live.
This article fixes two tolerance values (0m and 5m) side by side, in
both languages, to make the underlying algorithm easy to read from top
to bottom, and draws the resulting graph too, as a diagram below the
map.

No file uploaded? Both cells below fall back to the same eight-line
example: a closed block (four segments forming one connected loop), a
fully separate cluster elsewhere on the map, and a two-segment "spur"
whose first endpoint sits about 4m from the block's corner, not
exactly on it. That 4m gap is deliberately part of the example, not a
mistake in it: it's what section 3 below is about.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #network-from-lines-py}
#| package: geopandas, igraph
import numpy as np
import geopandas as gpd
import igraph as ig
from shapely.geometry import LineString, Point

# Same eight-line layout as the standalone tool's own example -- see
# the intro above for why the "spur" endpoint is offset on purpose.
FALLBACK_GEOMETRIES = [
    LineString([(12.4500, 41.9000), (12.4520, 41.9000)]),
    LineString([(12.4520, 41.9000), (12.4520, 41.9020)]),
    LineString([(12.4520, 41.9020), (12.4500, 41.9020)]),
    LineString([(12.4500, 41.9020), (12.4500, 41.9000)]),
    LineString([(12.45205, 41.9000), (12.4540, 41.9000)]),
    LineString([(12.4540, 41.9000), (12.4540, 41.9020)]),
    LineString([(12.4700, 41.9100), (12.4720, 41.9100)]),
    LineString([(12.4720, 41.9100), (12.4720, 41.9120)])
]

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
if gdf is None:
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=FALLBACK_GEOMETRIES, crs="EPSG:4326")
else:
    if gdf.crs is None:
        gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
        crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
    elif str(gdf.crs) != "EPSG:4326":
        gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")
    gdf = gdf[gdf.geometry.geom_type.isin(["LineString", "MultiLineString"])]

gdf = gdf.explode(index_parts=False).reset_index(drop=True)

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- same reasoning as this
# site's Buffer & Proximity and Viewshed articles: a snap tolerance in
# meters needs a projected CRS to mean an actual distance.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = (32600 if center_lat >= 0 else 32700) + utm_zone
gdf_proj = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)

# Endpoints only: interior vertices are a line's SHAPE, not its
# topology. Two per line -- ends[2*i] and ends[2*i+1] are line i's own
# start and end.
ends = np.array([
    c for geom in gdf_proj.geometry
    for c in (geom.coords[0][:2], geom.coords[-1][:2])
], dtype=float)


def build_graph(tolerance):
    """Snap endpoints within `tolerance` meters of each other into the
    same node, then build the graph. Same function, called twice below
    with two different tolerances -- the only thing that changes
    between the two results is this one number."""

    tol = max(tolerance, 1e-9)  # a tiny floor, not a literal 0, absorbs
                                 # floating-point noise between
                                 # coordinates meant to be identical.

    # Pairwise distances via plain numpy broadcasting, not a spatial
    # index -- fine at this scale, and keeps the two languages doing
    # the same recognizable thing line for line.
    diff = ends[:, None, :] - ends[None, :, :]
    dist = np.sqrt((diff ** 2).sum(axis=2))
    upper = np.triu(np.ones(dist.shape, dtype=bool), k=1)
    close_pairs = np.argwhere((dist <= tol) & upper)

    # Union-find: merges endpoints that are close enough into one
    # shared node id.
    parent = list(range(len(ends)))

    def find(i):
        while parent[i] != i:
            parent[i] = parent[parent[i]]
            i = parent[i]
        return i

    for a, b in close_pairs:
        ra, rb = find(int(a)), find(int(b))
        if ra != rb:
            parent[rb] = ra

    node_of = [find(i) for i in range(len(ends))]
    unique_nodes = sorted(set(node_of))
    node_index = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(unique_nodes)}

    edges = [
        (node_index[node_of[2 * i]], node_index[node_of[2 * i + 1]])
        for i in range(len(gdf_proj))
    ]

    g = ig.Graph(n=len(unique_nodes), edges=edges, directed=False)
    membership = list(g.connected_components().membership)

    # Everything below builds the graph's own geometry, for the diagram
    # panel further down -- kept inside this same function (not a
    # second computation) so the diagram always draws exactly the graph
    # these counts describe. Node representative = the MEAN of its
    # snapped members, so a snapped junction sits in their middle
    # instead of jumping to whichever line happened to be read first.
    reps = {}
    for i, n in enumerate(node_of):
        reps.setdefault(node_index[n], []).append(ends[i])

    node_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        {"node": list(range(len(unique_nodes))), "component": membership},
        geometry=[Point(np.mean(reps[i], axis=0)) for i in range(len(unique_nodes))],
        crs=gdf_proj.crs
    ).to_crs("EPSG:4326")

    edge_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
        {
            "source": [u for u, v in edges],
            "target": [v for u, v in edges],
            "component": [membership[u] for u, v in edges]
        },
        geometry=list(gdf_proj.geometry),
        crs=gdf_proj.crs
    ).to_crs("EPSG:4326")

    return {
        "nodes": g.vcount(),
        "edges": g.ecount(),
        "components": len(g.connected_components()),
        "nodeFeatures": node_gdf.__geo_interface__,
        "edgeFeatures": edge_gdf.__geo_interface__
    }


{
    "features": gdf.__geo_interface__,
    "crsWarning": crs_warning,
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "at0m": build_graph(0),
    "at5m": build_graph(5)
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #network-from-lines-r}
#| package: sf, igraph, geojsonsf, jsonlite
library(sf)
library(igraph)
library(geojsonsf)

# Same eight-line layout as the Python tab -- see the intro above for
# why the "spur" endpoint is offset on purpose.
fallback_geom <- st_sfc(
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4500, 41.9000), c(12.4520, 41.9000))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4520, 41.9000), c(12.4520, 41.9020))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4520, 41.9020), c(12.4500, 41.9020))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4500, 41.9020), c(12.4500, 41.9000))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.45205, 41.9000), c(12.4540, 41.9000))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4540, 41.9000), c(12.4540, 41.9020))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4700, 41.9100), c(12.4720, 41.9100))),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4720, 41.9100), c(12.4720, 41.9120))),
  crs = 4326
)

data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (is.null(data)) {
  data <- st_sf(geometry = fallback_geom)
} else if (is.na(st_crs(data))) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!isTRUE(st_crs(data) == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}
data <- data[st_geometry_type(data) %in% c("LINESTRING", "MULTILINESTRING"), ]
data <- st_cast(st_cast(data, "MULTILINESTRING"), "LINESTRING", warn = FALSE)

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- same reasoning as this
# site's Buffer & Proximity and Viewshed articles: a snap tolerance in
# meters needs a projected CRS to mean an actual distance.
bnd <- st_bbox(data)
center_lon <- (bnd[["xmin"]] + bnd[["xmax"]]) / 2
center_lat <- (bnd[["ymin"]] + bnd[["ymax"]]) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone
data_proj <- st_transform(data, calc_epsg)

# Endpoints only: interior vertices are a line's SHAPE, not its
# topology. Two rows per line -- row 2*i-1 and row 2*i are line i's
# own start and end (1-indexed, R-style).
ends <- do.call(rbind, lapply(st_geometry(data_proj), function(geom) {
  coords <- st_coordinates(geom)[, c("X", "Y"), drop = FALSE]
  rbind(coords[1, ], coords[nrow(coords), ])
}))

build_graph <- function(tolerance) {
  # Snap endpoints within `tolerance` meters of each other into the
  # same node, then build the graph. Same function, called twice below
  # with two different tolerances -- the only thing that changes
  # between the two results is this one number.

  tol <- max(tolerance, 1e-9)  # a tiny floor, not a literal 0, absorbs
                                # floating-point noise between
                                # coordinates meant to be identical.

  # Pairwise distances via a plain distance matrix, not a spatial
  # index -- fine at this scale, and keeps the two languages doing the
  # same recognizable thing line for line.
  n <- nrow(ends)
  dist_mat <- as.matrix(dist(ends))

  # Union-find: merges endpoints that are close enough into one shared
  # node id. Named uf_parent, not parent -- plain `parent` silently
  # resolved to an unrelated function from one of the loaded packages
  # instead of this vector, confirmed empirically (a real "object of
  # type 'closure' is not subsettable" error, not a hypothetical risk).
  # Only the nested find() needs <<- (it writes into build_graph's
  # scope from one level down); the loop below already runs in that
  # same scope, so it assigns with a plain <-.
  uf_parent <- seq_len(n)
  find <- function(i) {
    while (uf_parent[i] != i) {
      uf_parent[i] <<- uf_parent[uf_parent[i]]
      i <- uf_parent[i]
    }
    i
  }
  for (i in seq_len(n - 1)) {
    for (j in seq((i + 1), n)) {
      if (dist_mat[i, j] <= tol) {
        ri <- find(i)
        rj <- find(j)
        if (ri != rj) uf_parent[rj] <- ri
      }
    }
  }

  node_of <- vapply(seq_len(n), find, integer(1))
  unique_nodes <- sort(unique(node_of))
  node_index <- setNames(seq_along(unique_nodes), unique_nodes)

  n_lines <- nrow(data_proj)
  edges <- integer(0)
  for (i in seq_len(n_lines)) {
    edges <- c(
      edges,
      node_index[[as.character(node_of[2 * i - 1])]],
      node_index[[as.character(node_of[2 * i])]]
    )
  }

  g <- make_graph(edges, n = length(unique_nodes), directed = FALSE)
  membership <- components(g)$membership

  # Everything below builds the graph's own geometry, for the diagram
  # panel further down -- kept inside this same function (not a second
  # computation) so the diagram always draws exactly the graph these
  # counts describe. Node representative = the MEAN of its snapped
  # members, so a snapped junction sits in their middle instead of
  # jumping to whichever line happened to be read first. `edges` above
  # is already a flat (source1, target1, source2, target2, ...) vector
  # of graph vertex ids, so line i's source/target are just its two
  # entries -- no need to look node_of/node_index up a second time.
  node_points <- lapply(seq_along(unique_nodes), function(i) {
    members <- ends[node_of == unique_nodes[i], , drop = FALSE]
    st_point(colMeans(members))
  })
  node_sf <- st_transform(
    st_sf(
      node = seq_along(unique_nodes),
      component = membership,
      geometry = st_sfc(node_points, crs = calc_epsg)
    ),
    4326
  )

  edge_source <- edges[seq(1, 2 * n_lines, by = 2)]
  edge_target <- edges[seq(2, 2 * n_lines, by = 2)]
  edge_sf <- st_transform(
    st_sf(
      edge = seq_len(n_lines),
      source = edge_source,
      target = edge_target,
      component = membership[edge_source],
      geometry = st_geometry(data_proj)
    ),
    4326
  )

  list(
    nodes = jsonlite::unbox(vcount(g)),
    edges = jsonlite::unbox(ecount(g)),
    components = jsonlite::unbox(components(g)$no),
    nodeFeatures = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(node_sf, simplify = FALSE), simplifyVector = FALSE),
    edgeFeatures = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(edge_sf, simplify = FALSE), simplifyVector = FALSE)
  )
}

result <- list(
  # simplify = FALSE: sf_geojson()'s default (TRUE) returns a bare
  # vector of individual GeoJSON geometries instead of one
  # FeatureCollection when the sf object has no attribute columns --
  # exactly this article's fallback data (geometry only, no other
  # columns) -- forced off so the shape matches Python's
  # __geo_interface__ (always a FeatureCollection) regardless.
  features = jsonlite::fromJSON(sf_geojson(data, simplify = FALSE), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning),
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  at0m = build_graph(0),
  at5m = build_graph(5)
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

```{ojs}
// Same palette the standalone tool colors its own graph with
// (WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE, shared/ui.js) -- one color per connected
// component, so "how many colors" is a direct visual answer to "how

componentColor = (f) => WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE[(f.properties.component ?? 0) % WebGeoDS.DEFAULT_PALETTE.length]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
// Draws the map + both diagrams from WHICHEVER language's result comes
// in first -- called from both the Python and the R effect cells
// below, so a reader who runs only one language (in either order)
// still sees the map and the graphs, not a silently empty page.
// Harmless if both run: the second call just redraws the same picture
// the first one already drew, since Python and R compute the
// identical graph.
drawNetwork = async (result) => {
  mutable crsWarning = result.crsWarning;
  await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("network-from-lines-map", result.features, { paint: LINE_MAP_PAINT });
  await sharedMap.fitToData(result.features);

  graph0m.instance?.destroy();
  graph0m.instance = WebGeoDS.renderForceGraph(
    graph0m.box,
    { nodes: result.at0m.nodeFeatures, links: result.at0m.edgeFeatures },
    { nodeColor: componentColor, linkColor: componentColor }
  );
  graph5m.instance?.destroy();
  graph5m.instance = WebGeoDS.renderForceGraph(
    graph5m.box,
    { nodes: result.at5m.nodeFeatures, links: result.at5m.edgeFeatures },
    { nodeColor: componentColor, linkColor: componentColor }
  );
}
```

```{ojs}
    return wrap;

  row("Calculation CRS", s.calculationCrs);
  row("At 0m — nodes / edges / components", `${s.at0m.nodes} / ${s.at0m.edges} / ${s.at0m.components}`);
  row("At 5m — nodes / edges / components", `${s.at5m.nodes} / ${s.at5m.edges} / ${s.at5m.components}`);

  return wrap;
}
```

## 3. Same lines, two different answers

The numbers above describe the built-in fallback specifically. If you
uploaded your own file, the counts will differ, but the same effect is
what to look for. Both languages ran the exact same two tolerances (0m
and 5m) on the exact same eight lines, and got the same shape of
answer:

- **At 0m**, the "spur" (two segments starting about 4m from the
  block's corner) counts as its own piece: three components in total,
  the block, the spur, and the fully separate cluster.
- **At 5m**, that 4m gap is within tolerance, so the spur's near
  endpoint merges into the block's corner: two components, the
  now-joined block+spur, and the still-separate cluster.

Nothing about the geometry changed between the two runs: same
coordinates, same lines. Only the *definition of "the same point"*
changed, and that alone was enough to change how many pieces the
network has. This is why real-world network analysis (road networks,
utility networks, hydrology) always involves a noding/snapping step
before anything else: the raw geometry rarely already agrees with
itself down to the last centimeter, and the tolerance you pick is a
real analytical decision, not a technicality to skip past.

  tolerance you control live, and lets you download the result.
- **Wondering why the coordinate system needed picking at all?** →
  [Coordinate Reference Systems](crs-mismatch.qmd) covers the
  geographic/projected distinction this article leaned on in section 2.
